newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate considers bill that "castrates" FDA.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate considers bill that "castrates" FDA.

text.p: A consumer group lashed out on Thursday at moves by the U.S. Senate to pass a bill they said would "castrate" the Food and Drug Administration (FDA).
The Senate was expected to vote next month on a measure that a former editor of a respected medical journal said would take away much of the FDA's authority.

"This bill is not designed to improve the FDA. It's to castrate it, get it out of the regulatory business," Dr. Arnold Relman, former editor of the New England Journal of Medicine, said on Thursday at a news conference by the Public Citizen consumer group.
The measure was expected to come before the full Senate in September, Joe Karpinsky, a spokesman for the Labor and Human Resources Committee, said. He added it was voted out of the committee 14-4.

The bill would expand the FDA's use of third parties to review new medical devices, allow food labels to include health claims by scientific government agencies other than the FDA, and expedite access to some drugs or devices still under FDA review to patients facing life-threatening illnesses.

The measure is needed to reauthorize the Prescription Drug User Fee Act (PDURA) that expires on Sept 30. That act allows the FDA to collect fees from the drug companies to underwrite the costs of reviewing new prescription drug applications.

But Sen. Jack Reed, Rhode Island Democrat, who along with Sen. Edward Kennedy, Massachusetts Democrat, voted against the bill, told Reuters he wanted to see the final language, which was still being negotiated, and was concerned "especially about third-party reviews of medical devices ... and off-label drugs."

Phen-Fen, a new drug combination said to aid weight loss, is an example of off-label uses, Dr. Relman said. "Both drugs were approved by the FDA for other purposes. There never has been FDA approval of using those two drugs together to lose weight. Now, we know that there are a number of people who developed fatal disease of the lungs and heart," he said. "Allowing drug companies to market directly to doctors is very dangerous."

Sen. Judd Gregg, New Hampshire Republican, a supporter of the bill, said it will ensure the public will "have access to the highest quality medicines and technologies, the safest food and the best information about all of these products."

But Joan Claybrook, president of the public interest group Public Citizen, which has strongly opposed the measure, said the drug and medical device industry had contributed $34 million to various Senate campaigns over the last six years and there has been no hearing on the bill.

"There has been a general FDA hearing, but they kept this one quite secret. The final language isn't even available," she said, adding the bill "puts industry in the driver's seat much of the time and relegates the FDA to the back seat."
